Hello everyone, and thanks for inviting me to talk about my year as a language assistant. My name's Fernanda, and I'm from Curitiba in Brazil. Last September I moved to a small town in the south of Germany to help teach Portuguese and Spanish in a secondary school.

To be honest, the first few weeks were hard. I had studied German for three years, but people in the town spoke with a strong local accent, and I understood almost nothing at the bakery! I also didn't know anyone, and the town was very quiet in the evenings, especially compared to my home city.

Things got better when one of the teachers invited me to join the school choir. I'm not a great singer, but it was a fantastic way to meet people, and after rehearsals we often went out for something to eat. By November I had a small group of friends, and my German was improving every day.

In the classroom, my job was to help students practise speaking. I usually worked with groups of five or six students while the main teacher taught the rest of the class. At first the students were shy, so I started bringing Brazilian music and recipes to the lessons. That really helped. They were much more relaxed when we talked about food!

If you're thinking of applying, my main advice is this: don't just stay in your flat when you feel lonely. Say yes to every invitation, even if it's something you've never tried before. And don't worry too much about making mistakes in the language. People are usually very patient.

I'm now back in Brazil, finishing my degree, but I'm planning to return to Germany next year to do a master's in education. So, does anyone have any questions?

A: Today I'm joined by Aisha Bello, who has spent the last two years studying food waste in restaurant kitchens. Aisha, why restaurants in particular?
B: Well, households actually throw away more food overall, but restaurants are where small changes can have a big effect quickly. One manager can change the habits of a whole kitchen overnight, whereas persuading millions of households is a much slower process.
A: And what did you find was the biggest source of waste?
B: Most people assume it's what customers leave on their plates. That's part of it, but in the kitchens we studied, the larger share came from preparation: vegetables trimmed too heavily, sauces made in batches that were far too large, that kind of thing.
A: So the problem starts before the customer even sits down.
B: Exactly. And it's largely invisible, because nobody is measuring it. In one restaurant in Manchester, we simply put a set of scales next to the bins and asked staff to weigh everything they threw away. Within a month, waste had dropped by almost a third, without any other changes.
A: Just from weighing it? That's remarkable.
B: It is, although I should say it doesn't work everywhere. In very busy kitchens, staff saw the weighing as one more task, and some quietly stopped doing it after a few weeks. So it really needs a manager who believes in it.
A: What about portion sizes? Some people argue restaurants should simply serve less.
B: I'm cautious about that. Customers often feel cheated if the plate looks smaller, and they may not come back. I'd rather see restaurants offer a choice of sizes, or be more generous with side dishes that can be refilled on request.
A: And for listeners who run a kitchen, what's the first step?
B: Measure before you change anything. You can't fix what you can't see.

content.audio:
Over the past two decades, citizen science has moved from the margins of research to something close to the mainstream. Volunteers now count birds, classify galaxies from telescope images, record when plants first flower and monitor water quality in rivers. Some of these projects involve hundreds of thousands of people, and their data have appeared in leading scientific journals.

The usual case for citizen science rests on two claims. The first is that it allows research on a scale no professional team could manage. That claim is, I think, simply true. A single university group could never record bird numbers across an entire continent every spring. The second claim is that taking part makes the public more scientifically literate, and here I'd urge a little more caution. The evidence is surprisingly thin. Many volunteers already have a strong interest in science before they join, so it's hard to say whether participation is changing anyone's understanding or merely attracting people who were already well informed.

Then there's the question of data quality, which critics tend to raise first. In practice, though, this concern has largely been addressed. Well-designed projects build in checks: several volunteers classify the same image, or unusual records are flagged for an expert to review. In a number of comparisons, the combined judgements of volunteers have matched those of professionals remarkably closely.

What worries me more is something that rarely gets discussed: the question of credit. When a project leads to a significant discovery, volunteers are often thanked collectively in a footnote, while the professional researchers build their careers on the results. I'm not suggesting that every volunteer should be listed as an author. But if we want people to keep giving their time, we need to think harder about what they get in return, whether that's recognition, access to the findings, or a genuine say in which questions are asked in the first place.

So my argument is not that citizen science is overrated. It's that we've been praising it for the wrong reasons, and paying too little attention to the people who make it possible.

content.passage:
The bicycle library

When Wanjiru Kamau retired from her job as a primary school teacher, she expected to spend her days in her garden. Instead, at the age of sixty-two, she now spends three mornings a week riding a bicycle around the villages near her town in western Kenya, with two large boxes of books tied to the back.

The idea came to her almost by accident. A former student, now a mother of three, visited her one afternoon and mentioned that her children had nothing to read at home. The nearest library was more than fifteen kilometres away, and the bus was too expensive to take every week. "I had hundreds of books on my shelves that nobody was reading," Wanjiru says. "It seemed silly to keep them."

At first she simply lent books to the families she knew. But news spread quickly, and within a few months she had a list of more than eighty children who wanted to borrow something. Carrying the books on foot became impossible, so her nephew repaired an old bicycle for her and built the wooden boxes.

The project is not without its difficulties. During the rainy season, some of the roads turn to mud, and Wanjiru has to push the bicycle for long distances. Books are sometimes returned damaged, or not returned at all. "I don't get angry about that," she says. "If a book is lost because a child loved it too much, that's not a bad thing."

Local teachers say the effect has been clear. Children who borrow books regularly are more confident when they read aloud in class, and several parents have started reading with their children in the evenings.

Wanjiru now receives boxes of books from people in Nairobi who have heard about her work, and a local business has offered to pay for a second bicycle. She hopes to find a younger volunteer to visit the villages she cannot reach herself.

"People ask me when I'm going to stop," she laughs. "I tell them: when the children stop asking for books."

content.passage:
Four days, same pay: one company's experiment

Eighteen months ago, a mid-sized logistics firm in Hamburg made an announcement that surprised its competitors: all 140 office staff would move to a four-day week, with no reduction in pay. The company's founder, Katrin Weber, admits that the decision was partly a gamble. "We were losing good people to larger firms that could offer higher salaries," she explains. "We couldn't compete on money, so we decided to compete on time."

The early results were encouraging. Sick days fell by around a quarter in the first six months, and the number of staff leaving the company dropped to its lowest level in a decade. Perhaps more surprisingly, the amount of work completed each week stayed roughly the same. Managers put this down largely to a ruthless approach to meetings: most were cut to twenty-five minutes, and any meeting without a written agenda was cancelled.

Not everything has gone smoothly, however. Customer service staff, who need to be available five days a week, work on a rota, and some complain that their day off rarely falls on a Friday, when most of their colleagues are away. "It sometimes feels like there are two companies," one team leader told me, "the people who get long weekends, and the people who cover for them."

There is also the question of intensity. Several employees I spoke to said that their four working days now feel noticeably more pressured than the five days used to. One analyst, Tunde Okoro, put it bluntly: "I've gained a day, but I've lost the quiet moments. There's no time to chat at the coffee machine any more." For some, that is a fair exchange. For others, the loss of informal conversation has made the office feel colder.

Weber is aware of these concerns but remains convinced that the experiment has been worthwhile. She points out that, in a recent staff survey, only two employees said they would prefer to return to the old system. Yet that figure, while striking, may not tell the whole story. Staff who joined the company because of the four-day week are unlikely to argue against it, and those who found the new rhythm hardest may already have left.

What the Hamburg experience suggests, perhaps, is not that a shorter week is right for every organisation, but that it changes more than the calendar. Firms considering the move would do well to think not only about which day people take off, but about what kind of workplace remains on the other four.

content.passage:
The tyranny of the recommendation

There was a time when discovering a new piece of music required a certain amount of effort. You might hear something on the radio in a friend's car, scribble down half a lyric, and spend weeks trying to track it down. The process was inefficient, often frustrating and, in retrospect, oddly rewarding. The song you eventually found felt as though it belonged to you.

Today, of course, the effort has largely disappeared. Streaming services analyse what we listen to and serve up an endless supply of similar tracks, often with uncanny accuracy. It would be churlish to deny the benefits. Listeners in small towns now have access to musical traditions from Lagos, Seoul and Sao Paulo that would once have been almost impossible to hear, and independent artists can reach audiences without the backing of a major record label.

Yet there is a growing body of opinion, which I largely share, that something has been lost in the bargain. Recommendation systems are, by design, conservative. They reward listeners for liking what they already like, and they nudge us gently towards the familiar. Over time, the effect may be less a widening of taste than a narrowing of it: a comfortable loop in which surprise becomes increasingly rare.

The counter-argument deserves a fair hearing. Defenders of these systems point out that people have always gravitated towards the familiar; radio stations played the same hits on repeat long before algorithms existed. They also note that listeners remain free to search for anything they wish. Both points are valid, as far as they go. But they overlook the enormous influence of the default option. Most of us, most of the time, take the path of least resistance, and when that path is laid out for us by a system designed to keep us listening, the freedom to wander off it is more theoretical than real.

None of this is an argument for returning to the days of crackling radio reception and half-remembered lyrics. Nostalgia is a poor guide to the future. What it does suggest is that listeners might benefit from cultivating a little deliberate inefficiency: following a recommendation from a friend rather than a machine, listening to an album from start to finish, or occasionally choosing something precisely because it seems unlikely to appeal.

Taste, after all, is not simply a set of preferences to be satisfied. It is something that grows, often through encounters we would never have chosen. The danger is not that machines will choose badly for us, but that they will choose too well, and leave us with nothing left to discover.
